title: Instance selection sim table & notes: A10 / L4 / A100 / H100
content:
Purpose:
Quick, actionable simulation + notes comparing instance classes (A10, L4, A100-80GB, H100-80GB) under three representative inference workloads. Goal: give product and infra teams a single-page decision path and a small simulated table to drive experiments and pricing recommendations.

Status: draft — numbers are simulated (workload-pattern-driven) and include coarse power assumptions. Treat as hypothesis: run meas experiments (see TODO).

Summary (one-line):
- For short-turn chat and embedding-heavy workloads, L4 tends to give the best $/1M tokens and perf/W.
- For very large-model long-context inference, H100 gives best raw throughput and perf/W but higher $/token unless reserved pricing or multi-GPU aggregation is used.

Assumptions used in these sims:
- Hourly instance/GPU costs (on-demand, cloud list): A10 = $0.95/hr, L4 = $0.80/hr, A100-80GB = $3.50/hr, H100-80GB = $7.00/hr.
- Nominal continuous GPU power (W): A10 = 175W, L4 = 120W, A100 = 400W, H100 = 450W.
- Warm-cache throughput; cold-cache penalty applied separately (see notes).
- Batching: default dynamic batching on (kernel-level XLA-like ops), but batch overhead reduces at high concurrency. Sim assumes efficient batching for embeddings and short-turn chat.
- Model sizes & kernels: small=7B, medium=33B, large=70B. Numbers below illustrate small (7B) and large (70B) extremes plus embedding workload.

Methodology (brief):
- Pick representative token/sec targets from internal microbench runs + kernel scaling curves.
- tokens/hr = tokens/sec * 3600.
- $/1M tokens = hourly_cost / tokens/hr * 1e6.
- perf/W = tokens/sec / power_draw.
- We simulate 3 workloads: short-chat (7B), long-context (70B), embeddings (small output).
- Note: these are single-GPU numbers; multi-GPU linearity and NVLink batching not modeled here.

Simulation table (single-GPU, warm cache)
Workload A — Short chat (7B, avg 40 tokens, bursty concurrency)
Instance | tokens/sec | tokens/hr | $/1M tokens | power W | perf/W (tok/s/W) | median latency @ concurrency 8 (ms) | p95 (ms)
A10      | 22,000    | 79,200,000 | $0.0120     | 175     | 125.7            | 52                              | 125
L4       | 28,000    |100,800,000 | $0.00794    | 120     | 233.3            | 38                              | 95
A100     | 60,000    |216,000,000 | $0.01620    | 400     | 150.0            | 25                              | 60
H100     | 95,000    |342,000,000 | $0.02047    | 450     | 211.1            | 18                              | 45

Interpretation: L4 lowest $/1M for short-turn generation due to favorable cost and high per-GPU throughput for smaller models. A100/H100 give much higher absolute throughput but worse $/token on on-demand pricing.

Workload B — Long-context generation (70B, avg 1024 input + 256 output)
Instance | tokens/sec | tokens/hr | $/1M tokens | power W | perf/W | median latency @ concurrency 4 (ms) | p95 (ms)
A10      | 1,800     | 6,480,000   | $0.1466     | 175     | 10.29  | 420                             | 760
L4       | 2,400     | 8,640,000   | $0.09259    | 120     | 20.00  | 330                             | 610
A100     | 7,000     |25,200,000   | $0.13889    | 400     | 17.50  | 140                             | 290
H100     | 12,000    |43,200,000   | $0.16204    | 450     | 26.67  | 90                              | 180

Interpretation: H100 has best perf/W and raw tokens/sec for large models, but L4 still competitive on $/1M under these assumed prices. For latency-sensitive long-context workloads with small fleets, A100/H100 may be preferable because they reduce tail latency and headroom for spikes.

Workload C — Embedding-heavy (many short requests, avg 8 tokens)
Instance | tokens/sec | tokens/hr | $/1M tokens | power W | perf/W | median latency @ concurrency 16 (ms) | p95 (ms)
A10      | 45,000    |162,000,000 | $0.00586    | 175     | 257.1  | 20                              | 50
L4       | 58,000    |208,800,000 | $0.00383    | 120     | 483.3  | 12                              | 35
A100     | 120,000   |432,000,000 | $0.00810    | 400     | 300.0  | 8                               | 20
H100     | 210,000   |756,000,000 | $0.00926    | 450     | 466.7  | 5                               | 12

Interpretation: Embedding throughput strongly favors L4 (best $/1M and perf/W). Batch aggregation efficiency on L4 is very high for short fixed-length workloads.

Sensitivity notes (high-level):
- Cold cache: assume warm->cold throughput drop: short-chat -10% (marginal), long-context -35% (KV cache regen), embeddings -5%. Cold-cache increases cost/token accordingly.
- Reserved pricing: 30–60% discount materially changes $/token ordering; run reserved sim if customer commit applies.
- Multi-GPU: H100/A100 scale better for extremely large models (70B+) where sharding reduces per-token flops; single-GPU numbers understate their advantage in multi-GPU setups.
- Quantization: INT8/4 reduces memory footprint and may increase tokens/sec on A100/L4; include in next experiments.

Decision guidance (quick):
- Default recommendation for general-purpose hosted API (mixed small/medium models, many short requests): L4-backed pools with autoscaling and aggressive batching.
- Embedding-dominant customers: choose L4 pools with high concurrency and batching windows, optimize prefetch and batching at gateway.
- Large-model, long-context customers (70B+): evaluate H100 or multi-A100 pools; prefer H100 for latency-critical SLAs and A100 for predictable $/token if using reserved pricing.
- If customers require lower unit cost and can accept slightly higher latency, consider A100 with larger batch windows + int8 profiles.

Operational recommendations / config knobs to run in the field:
- Default batching window: 8–12ms for short-chat, 4–6ms for embeddings (lower latency), 20–30ms for long-context to maximize throughput.
- KV cache retention policy: keep for 30–60s per user session to reduce cold-cache penalty on follow-ups.
- Quantization profile: expose int8/4 toggle in Optimize recommendations for compatible models.
- Autoscale: configure target utilization differently per instance (L4 target 55–70%, A100/H100 45–60% to maintain latency headroom).

Monte-Carlo sim notes (how numbers were produced):
- For each workload we sample concurrency (Poisson), sequence length (empirical distribution), and batch-filling efficiency (beta distribution).
- Kernel throughput curves applied per model/GPU type.
- Run 10k trials, report median throughput and 90th percentile latency.

Open questions / TODOs:
- [ ] Run controlled bench runs for the same docker runtime image across all four GPUs and capture actual power draw traces (SRE ticket JIRA-INF-912).
- [ ] Validate quantized kernels (int8) for target customer models and re-run sims with quantization uplift factor.
- [ ] Add reserved pricing scenarios (1yr, 3yr) and committed use discounts to spreadsheet and decision tree.
- [ ] Add multi-GPU sharded experiments for 70B+/seq length=32k workloads and NVLink scaling curves.

Notes to eng (measurement guidance):
- Use kernel-level perf counters + nvidia-smi power logging. Collect at 1s granularity for 5–10 minute runs at steady-state.
- Capture p95 latency with synthetic arrival process (Poisson lambda tuned to target concurrency).
- Ensure warm-cache runs by issuing warmup tokens for 30s prior to sample window.

References / links:
- Confluence: instance-selection-v2 (linked above)
- JIRA: JIRA-INF-912 (bench coordination)
- RFC: github.com/redwood-inference/rfcs/pull/78

Bottom line (single paragraph):
- For the majority of customer patterns we see in our hosted API (short-turn chat + embeddings), L4 gives the best mix of $/token and perf/W and should be the default pool for new small/medium model routes. For very large models or extreme long-context workloads that demand the lowest tail latency and highest per-request throughput, H100 (or sharded A100 clusters) is recommended despite higher on-demand $/token. Next step: validate these sims with an agreed 2-week bench plan and add reserved-cost cases to the decision matrix.

Author notes: rough draft; numbers intentionally coarse to guide experiments rather than final pricing. Drop comments or tag me in Slack #product-optimize for quick sync.
